item.title: GPT-6's new feature adds interactive elements to your chat, even if you're a free user
item.itunes:title: GPT-6's new feature adds interactive elements to your chat, even if you're a free user
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • GPT-6's Intelligent UI auto-generates interactive visuals (diagrams, tables, graphs) to clarify complex topics.
  • Examples include bicycle part diagrams, scalable roast planners, and receipt-based bill splitters.
  • Rolling out to Plus/Pro/Business/Enterprise today; Free and Go get it tomorrow.

One thing I really enjoy when using Gemini is the little interactive elements it will generate at times. I don't even need to ask for one; I'll ask for an overview comparing two things, or explaining a complex topic, and it will automatically generate a fun little diagram or chart I can click on to understand it more easily.

Now, OpenAI is introducing something similar to GPT-6. It's called Intelligent UI, and it aims to add a visual aid to whatever it's explaining at the time.

GPT-6's Intelligent UI breaks down complicated topics into easy-to-understand diagrams

They're looking very useful already

Credit: OpenAI

As announced on the OpenAI blog, the company is adding Intelligent UI to GPT-6. It seemingly works akin to Google Gemini's feature, where ChatGPT will detect when and where a diagram would be most useful, then create one on the fly, embedding it right within the chat window. Sometimes it's a table, sometimes it's a graph, and sometimes it's something you can mouse over and click on to learn more about things.

The examples OpenAI showed were pretty impressive, including a little diagram showing the components of a bicycle, a Sunday roast ingredients planner that you can scale yourself according to the number of visitors, and even an interactive clipboard-style panel for calculating who owes what at a restaurant, using data from a receipt photo.

The best part is, you won't need to wait long until you can use it, regardless of what tier you're on. It's releasing to the ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise tiers today, but those on the Free and Go plans need not worry, as they'll get it during a rollout tomorrow.

When GPT-6 Astra started losing at StarCraft, it just stole the winning bot instead of playing fair

Like a real gamer, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra wanted to win at all costs.

3
By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: A $5 ESP32 fixed every Bluetooth range problem in my Home Assistant setup
item.itunes:title: A $5 ESP32 fixed every Bluetooth range problem in my Home Assistant setup
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My living room temperature sensor kept showing as unavailable in Home Assistant. It didn’t happen every time, but often enough to break my smart fan automation. On checking, I learned that the sensor and its batteries were fine. The real problem was that my Home Assistant server sits in my bedroom, and the Bluetooth adapter doesn’t reach that far.

I fixed it with an ESP32 DevKit V1 board that cost me $5. If you want the steps to flashing steps, a Bluetooth proxy guide covers them, and you can then adjust the settings in the newer ESPHome interface. Running a single board made me realize one wasn’t enough, and I needed another proxy elsewhere in the house. To place that, you need to know where to place a proxy and when to add another one.

4 simple ESP32 projects you can build without any sensors

Not all ESP32 projects need to involve extra sensors or circuit components

By  Ayush Pande

Range problems show up before devices drop

Home Assistant’s advertisement monitor shows where coverage ends

Before placing any proxy, I opened the Bluetooth advertisement monitor which comes with the Bluetooth integration in Home Assistant. You can find it at /config/bluetooth/advertisement-monitor on your Home Assistant address and check what each device reported. Devices at the edge of coverage don’t go dark all at once. Their signal strength creeps down, and the dropouts follow.

My LG C2 read -86 dBm through the server’s adapter, and the Govee Table Lamp 2 read -85 dBm. Those were the two devices that kept dropping, while the ones near the server read about -67 to -77 dBm and never gave me trouble. Values closer to zero mean a stronger signal, so -67 dBm is much stronger than -86 dBm. That’s how I got numbers to monitor rather than vaguely chasing Bluetooth stability in my house.

A proxy between the server and the weak spot

Placing it away from the router keeps the signal clean

To address the dead zone, I wanted to place a proxy between my router and the weak spot so it could reach most devices. So I plugged the ESP32 DevKit V1 in near the other bedroom’s door, close to the dead zone. After that, I got better readings for the BLE devices sitting far away, the ones that’d just drop off and disappear. I also set its bluetooth_proxy value to active so it works as a two-way relay that lets Home Assistant send commands.

I placed another proxy in the same bedroom as Home Assistant instance running on a server, but a little farther from the router. I followed the warning in ESPHome’s documentation to keep the node away from my router and avoid degrading Bluetooth reception. Bluetooth and Wi-Fi also share the 2.4Ghz band, so a proxy placed next to the router competes with its own Wi-Fi link.

I moved the second proxy node between the router and the first node in the other bedroom. That sounds like a boring fix, but it settled the placement. The proxy gets a decent Wi-Fi signal and a clear path to the devices it covers. It doesn’t need to sit near the server. Recheck the advertisements monitor after each move, since even a small change in position can shift the readings.

Board choice changes range less than the placement does

ESP32 DevKit V1 and NodeMCU-32S gave nearly similar readings

I own an ESP32 DevKit V1 and a NodeMCU-32S development board. I tested both of them in the same spot with the same firmware. Both gave me similar readings, between -84 and -88 dBm, which was proof enough for me to pick one.

I also took the ESP32-C6 for a spin as a Bluetooth proxy since it carries a newer chip with Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.3 support. I couldn’t find anything showing that the newer chip reaches farther over Bluetooth. After all, range depends on the antenna and your home environment. I stuck with the DevKit V1 because it costs $5 and runs the stock ESPHome proxy firmware without extra work.

Distant rooms need their own proxy

Wi-Fi coverage and overlap decide where each board goes

My porch was a tough spot, and since it was far away from the Home Assistant instance, it never had a chance. Moving the first proxy closer fixed one dead zone but created another. So a second board in the problem area worked better than pushing one to its limits. To place it, I needed a strong Wi-Fi signal and a USB charger nearby to power it. A proxy dropping off Wi-Fi is useless no matter how good the Bluetooth is, so I checked Wi-Fi strength at the spot before mounting the node.

I now run two proxies and don’t aim to space them evenly. I placed them with enough overlap that a BLE device can reach either. Two boards in the same room would’ve cost the same and fixed nothing. Home Assistant pools every proxy and routes each device through one. So an extra proxy helps if it can reach devices the other proxy can’t.

4 simple ESP32 projects you can build without any sensors

Not all ESP32 projects need to involve extra sensors or circuit components

By  Ayush Pande

A cheap board fixed a placement problem

The ESP32 DevKit V1 costs just $5 and runs stock ESPHome firmware for a Bluetooth proxy. Placement fixed the dead zone, not the board. The temperature sensor that kept disappearing from Home Assistant is reachable now thanks to the Bluetooth proxy. Every BLE device on the other side of my bedroom is reachable, and their advertisements are stable now. If your Bluetooth devices keep dropping, check the signal readings and the proxy’s position before you blame the sensor or buy a more expensive board.

item.title: I switched back to Waze for one feature Google Maps still refuses to get right
item.itunes:title: I switched back to Waze for one feature Google Maps still refuses to get right
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Google Maps is my everyday go-to for navigation for its excellent database of businesses and opening hours, but lately I've been coming back to Waze much more often than I expected.

And it's all because of one Waze feature that makes route awareness so much better. You see, when I'm driving somewhere unfamiliar, knowing that I'm going to run into traffic is only part of the story. I want to know why traffic is slow, whether a lane is blocked or there's an accident, so I can plan around it.

That's where Waze's crowdsourced reporting makes a huge difference. Drivers can report crashes, hazards, police sightings, and much more directly from the car. These reports immediately show up for other drivers approaching the same route. Make no mistake: Google Maps lets you do the same.

However, Waze's hyperactive user base is what makes it work. After all, an app dependent on user reports is only as good as its active user base.

I used Waze and Google Maps side by side, and one quickly became my favorite

Google Maps gets you there, but Waze warns you what's waiting

7
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Waze helps me make better route decisions

Community feedback makes the alerts useful

The biggest benefit of Waze's reports is that they let me plan my route better. Unless I'm on the expressway, there are usually multiple routes to my destination. Often, these are routes a navigation app won't pick on its own.

When Waze shows me that there's an accident ahead, I can take a Waze-suggested alternate route, my own preferred route, or, in an extreme scenario. Yes, I've been there, parked my car, and chilled at a coffee shop for a bit instead of sticking around in traffic for an hour or two.

Hazard reports are just as useful, if not more so. Recently, I was stuck for three hours on a route that usually takes me 45 minutes. The reason? A bus that had broken down. Knowing this ahead of time would've helped me plan better. In fact, this incident played a big role in me actively checking Waze more often than before.

Using Waze also helps you create a feedback loop. Yes, I'm consuming information shared by other users. However, the app makes it easy enough to contribute back, even using Android Auto. It's been helpful that I've been self-motivated enough to share back with the community. This community element is what makes Waze so much more useful than Google Maps.

Waze gives you a heads-up about what's coming up ahead

Better situational awareness

When I'm out on a long road trip, avoiding redundancy in navigation is crucial. That's another reason why Waze is quickly becoming my go-to. Many third-party navigation apps, like Organic Maps or Magic Earth, can tell me where to go. That's a solved problem. But few can give me a heads-up about what the journey will be like.

When you start navigation, Google Maps gives you a broad idea of the route you'll take and how long it'll take. But you only find potential interruptions once you start driving.

Waze tells you about these interruptions ahead of time. I can glance at the map and see all the reports along the route before I start driving, or even while I'm on the road. If I see several incident reports clustered around a single stretch of the road, that's a dead giveaway that I'm going to run into delays. But what matters is having enough information to decide whether to follow the suggested route or take a different one.

Credit: 

In addition to the larger warnings that can cause significant route disruptions or make you change your route, I also like the smaller warnings Waze provides. Waze can alert me to things such as speed bumps, sharp curves, railway crossings, and changes in the speed limits.

Put together, using Waze gives me a lot of situational awareness. Like any crowdsourced tool, you have to treat it as another source of information to make a more informed decision. If the app warns you of something on the road, keep in mind the incident report might not be recent, and the object might no longer be there. More importantly, the app counts on you to improve the data set by updating those reports as you drive further. Thanks to Android Auto, that's incredibly easy and can be done right there from your car's infotainment system.

Waze augments Google Maps but doesn't replace it

For me, Waze's appeal isn't that it's a Google Maps replacement. In many ways, it is not. Google Maps remains the map app I use when I need to figure out my destination or know whether the store will even be open by the time I get there.

Waze serves a different purpose. It gives me route awareness and a running stream of information about the road itself. And the best part is that this information comes from other people who are riding that same road.

I turned an old phone into a permanent Android Auto device, and my main phone never connects to the car anymore

My Pixel 8 Pro is now my dedicated Android Auto device.

item.title: Microsoft's new Surface RTX Spark Dev Box ships with a "ready-to-code Windows experience" and a hefty price tag
item.itunes:title: Microsoft's new Surface RTX Spark Dev Box ships with a "ready-to-code Windows experience" and a hefty price tag
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • The Surface RTX Spark Dev Box ships with Project Zenith.
  • Price: $6,000 — a hefty premium for a dev-focused machine.
  • Specs: Nvidia RTX Spark N1X (6144-core GPU), 20-core CPU, 128GB RAM, 2TB SSD; preorder now.

Back in June, Microsoft gave us the first look at what it calls the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box. It didn't reveal everything at the time, but the company has looped back around to it during this year's Windows and Surface event.

As it turns out, this dev box will ship with a version of Windows designed with developers in mind, and it comes at a pretty huge price tag.

Microsoft's Surface RTX Spark Dev Box will run Project Zenith and costs $6,000

You might need to break open the piggy bank for this one

Credit: Microsoft / YouTube / Screenshot

Earlier today, Microsoft held a Windows and Surface event where it dropped several notable announcements, including new Copilot-enhanced Windows Search and the Surface Laptop Ultra. However, it also took some time to revisit the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, a device Microsoft says users have been asking for ever since it was revealed at Build.

The announcement was pretty brief and consisted of two key points. First, the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box will run on Project Zenith, which Microsoft described as "a ready-to-code Windows experience, pre-configured out-of-the-box so you can build from day one." We heard about this back in early September, and it seems the tech giant is ready to begin shipping units with it.

Second, the price tag. The RTX Spark Dev Box will set you back $6,000, and it's easy to see why. It's running off an Nvidia RTX Spark with a 20-core CPU and a Blackwell GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores. It also comes with 128GB of memory and a 2TB SSD to keep everything running smoothly.

If the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box still sounds like a winner to you, you can pre-order one right now via the Microsoft Discover Surface website, with shipping starting in November.

We finally know the Surface Laptop Ultra’s price and release date, and how its clever breakaway USB-C port works

The Nvidia RTX-powered laptop starts at $2,600 and ships on October 16th.

item.title: ECC memory isn't the NAS requirement people make it out to be, and there are better ways to protect your data
item.itunes:title: ECC memory isn't the NAS requirement people make it out to be, and there are better ways to protect your data
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Seeing as how the primary objective of Network-Attached Storage servers is to store backups and archived data, they don’t sound all that complicated at first glance. However, it wasn’t until I built my first NAS that I came across all the software jargon and unique components that are typically required for a reliable storage server.

On the popular side of things, you’ve got hot spares, rsync workloads, scrub tasks, SLOG devices, and a bunch of other useful ways to improve your NAS’ functionality. Many folks consider ECC memory an important part of this group, and I used to be one of them until a few years ago. Although there are certain benefits to these RAM kits, their sky-high price tags make them far less tempting for simple consumer-tier home servers, especially when you can add cheaper (and to some extent, better) upgrades to your NAS.

My NAS backup strategy costs $0 a month, and it's more reliable than any cloud service I've tested

It's pretty easy to set up, too

25
By  Ayush Pande

ECC memory is undoubtedly helpful for hardcore NAS units

It’s an extra safeguard against data corruption

When you’ve got TBs of data stored on your NAS, you’ll want to take extra precautions to stop corruption from rearing its ugly head. Failed transfer tasks, improper shutdowns, and damaged hardware are typically the most common causes of file corruption, but bit rot is another problem that can cause your data to become irretrievable. The problem? Bit rot can gradually corrupt your data during normal NAS operations, and without proper failsafes, you won’t notice until it’s too late.

After all, anything from magnetic decay on HDDs and high temps to manufacturing defects and cosmic rays can trigger bit rot, and that’s where Error-Correcting Code memory comes into the equation. Unlike normal, consumer-tier memory, ECC RAM bears nine chips instead of the usual eight, and it uses this extra chip to add seven extra bits for each block of data. The sole purpose of these extra bits is ensuring data integrity, so when a single bit of actual data changes due to bit rot, the ECC memory detects it and flips it right back.

Since bit rot can slowly corrupt your storage pools over time, it can snowball into unrecoverable data if you’re not careful. ECC memory serves as a solid counter to this problem, which is why it’s borderline essential for enterprise servers. Back in the day, I used to consider it pretty useful for backup workstations, but things have changed a lot since then.

That said, it’s still an optional upgrade for consumer home labs

It’s also not very feasible considering the current RAM prices

When I got my first 64GB DDR4 ECC memory kit, it barely cost $150, even with all the shipping costs. Considering that typical DDR4 memory would’ve cost around $15-20 less, this investment wasn’t all that expensive since it would add an additional layer of protection between my data and bit rot. But since the RAM apocalypse is still in full swing, even traditional memory kits have become overpriced. Considering ECC memory is designed for production-grade servers, you can imagine how expensive it’s gotten in this day and age.

Fortunately, ECC memory isn’t the only way to detect bit rot. Plenty of modern NAS distributions support scrub tasks, which use checksums to look for corruption. For the uninitiated, a checksum is a unique identifier created for each block of data transferred to a storage pool. When you run a scrub task, your NAS distro recalculates the checksum and compares it to the original value. Since bit rot (or any other form of corruption, for that matter) causes changes to the new value of the checksum, the scrub task detects the faulty block immediately.

Of course, scrub tasks can’t really fix bit rot on their own. But if you run them every once in a while and have enough backups, you can restore your data to its former uncorrupted glory.

Your NAS should snapshot more often, and here's what I do and why

Snapshots are a solid way to safeguard your precious data

2
By  Ayush Pande

Personally, I’d choose a 3-2-1 backup over ECC memory

A remote NAS is more reassuring than a local high-end storage server

Going back to the cost analysis of ECC memory, there are still plenty of problems these overpriced RAM sticks can’t solve. For example, failing hard drives can easily cause my backup and archival data to become irrecoverable, regardless of the amount of ECC memory in my NAS. Likewise, no amount of ECC memory can protect my storage pools from ransomware, accidental deletions, or random natural disasters.

So, if I really have to invest in a safeguard for my NAS, I’d go for a 3-2-1 backup pipeline before I go anywhere near ECC kits. That’s because remote NAS servers lying hundreds of miles away from my home lab can not only protect my data from all these untoward scenarios, but they even serve as a reliable counter to bit rot.

The best part? They don’t have to be expensive, either. Depending on the amount of data you consider “essential,” these remote servers can be as cheap as simple 2-bay NAS rigs that use simple rsync tasks to pull specific storage pools from your local NAS.

item.title: Atlas VTT turns Obsidian into a full virtual tabletop, and it's free to use offline
item.itunes:title: Atlas VTT turns Obsidian into a full virtual tabletop, and it's free to use offline
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Obsidian has become my go-to manager for my DnD campaigns. It's an excellent tool for tracking where my players are in the story, what items they have, and managing the dozens of loose threads I can pull to add a bit of variety to the game. That's especially true in long-running campaigns like Dungeon of the Mad Mage. I use Roll20 for the actual gameplay and damage calculations, but Obsidian is my digital notebook for keeping track of everything.

But now? Roll20 might be a thing of the past. A new plugin called Atlas VTT (Virtual Tabletop) brings many of those same Roll20 features right into Obsidian, including a separate view for players and DMs. It's honestly one of the most impressive Obsidian plugins I've seen, and that's saying something, considering how many I've experimented with.

Atlas VTT began as a passion project but has grown into much more

It's everything tabletop players need, built by someone who understands them

On Atlas VTT's Obsidian plugin page, the creator states that "[He] built Atlas as part of my bachelor's thesis to give the TTRPG community a virtual tabletop that's open source, hackable, and free to use." Fabian Urbanek has essentially created a platform like Roll20, but it gives dungeon masters and players nearly complete control. Everything happens inside the Obsidian vault. There's no third-party processing, which means far fewer privacy concerns, and the level of customization is insanely impressive.

It works well with several other tools, like the Fantasy Statblock plugin. The features you expect from a tool like this are all present and accounted for: DMs can measure distances, hide parts of the map, track turns and initiative, and even choose specific musical tracks for different battles. Right now, Atlas VTT only works on desktop. While I haven't seen confirmation that it's coming to mobile versions of Obsidian, it feels like the next natural evolution of this tool.

I can't believe it, but this Obsidian plugin is fantastic for playing D&D and other tabletop games

Makes planning campaigns a breeze.

3
By  Simon Batt

It's game-agnostic, with built-in support for multiple formats

It's more than just DnD 5e

A huge number of people have come to tabletop gaming through Dungeons and Dragons, and that's not a bad thing. It's probably the most well-known TTRPG in history, but there are so many more systems to pick from. Atlas VTT lets you choose from DnD 5e, Daggerheart, Call of Cthulhu, Cyberpunk RED, and more. And if none of those fit the bill? You can create your own system, setting specific measurement units, distance per square, movement settings, and even how the game handles diagonal movement. Once created, you can choose that system later when you want to start a new campaign in the same setting. It's also a great way to implement systems that aren't included by default.

Atlas VTT goes beyond just movement tweaks. It also supports different conditions that affect how the game is played, like Call of Cthulhu's Bout of Madness or Pathfinder's Clumsy condition. You can create custom conditions, but many common choices are included and visible when you select the system. For example, D&D 5e has 15 conditions and 6 senses, while Call of Cthulhu has 9 conditions.

Campaign notes become part of the map

Where Obsidian's note-taking comes in

One of my biggest complaints with Roll20 is how clunky and disconnected the map can feel from the actual gameplay. Navigating the obtuse menus is time-consuming, especially when I'm trying to reference something in the middle of a session quickly. Sure, there are shortcuts — double-clicking an icon to bring up the stat page is one way of doing it — but when I'm trying to check what's in a specific room ahead of my players arriving there, I usually just flip open the physical campaign book rather than trying to find it in Roll20. item.title: We finally know the Surface Laptop Ultra’s price and release date, and how its clever breakaway USB-C port works
item.itunes:title: We finally know the Surface Laptop Ultra’s price and release date, and how its clever breakaway USB-C port works
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • The Surface Laptop Ultra starts at $2,600, and pre-orders are open now, with a ship date of October 16th.
  • Microsoft says the powerful laptop has been built around Nvidia's RTX Spark, with local AI, creative workflows, and high-end gaming in mind.
  • The tech giant says the Surface Laptop Ultra is capable of 99% of its overall power while running on battery.

At Computex back in May, Microsoft first showed off the Surface Laptop Ultra, its new laptop powered by Nvidia's ARM-based RTX Spark chip. While we got a decent look at its sleek design at the time, it was still unclear how much it would cost or when it would be released.

Fast-forward a couple of months to Microsoft's first Surface event in a few years, and we now know the high-end Surface Laptop Ultra starts at $2,600 and that it's available to pre-order now, with a launch date of October 16th. The laptop has long been positioned by Microsoft as the most powerful Windows 11 laptop out there, with the tech giant emphasizing that it can easily handle everything from local AI computing to creative workloads and high-end gaming, thanks to its powerful RTX Spark chip.

With the Surface Laptop Ultra's power and the ongoing memory shortage in mind, it's not entirely surprising that its entry-level price landed at $2,600. The Surface Laptop Ultra's base configuration features a 15-inch mini-LED screen, a sizable haptic trackpad, three USB-C ports (and one of them features a unique magnetic breakaway design), 24GB of RAM, and Nvidia's 18-core RTX Spark Arm CPU and a Blackwell GPU with 5,120 CUDA cores.

Microsoft showed off the Surface Laptop Ultra's breakaway magnetic USB-C port for the first time

The tech giant says the laptop was built from the ground up for the RTX Spark

During the Surface keynote, Microsoft revealed other interesting details about the powerful laptop, including that it features "the world's first built-in magnetic USB-C charging." The new magnetic charger looks sort of like Apple's MacBook MagSafe power connector, but built on the more open USB-C standard. The tech giant also confirmed that the Surface Laptop Ultra can maintain 99% of its power when running off its battery, ensuring users still have access to nearly all the RTX Spark's power when on the go.

As expected, the tech giant also talked up the Surface Laptop's AI capabilities, with EVP of Windows and DevicesPavan Davuluri emphasizing that the company "built the Surface Laptop Ultra around Nvidia's RTX Spark." He added that users "can run models on this laptop that simply don't fit on a traditional machine."

During the keynote, Microsoft confirmed that several games will run on the ARM-based RTX Spark at launch, including the recently released Gears of War: E-Day, along with World of Warcraft: Forever, Arc Raiders, Cyberpunk, and several more. Given the powerful laptop's Nvidia Blackwell GPU, this is pretty expected, but it's still reassuring to see Microsoft emphasize the Surface Laptop Ultra's gaming capabilities.

The Call of Duty series coming to the Surface Laptop Ultra and the RTX Spark in 2027 was far more surprising. This means Activision's Ricochet anti-cheat will soon run on ARM64 devices (Activision is owned by Microsoft). That said, it's unclear whether Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is coming to the RTX Spark first or will end up being next year's Call of Duty title.

Along with confirming the Surface Laptop Ultra's price and pre-order date, Microsoft also revealed that the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box starts at $6,000.

Creating the ultimate Zigbee network

I rely on one of these to help run the entire smart home. With this Sonoff dongle running alongside Home Assistant, I can connect Zigbee devices to Home Assistant with a dedicated network. Windows 11 traces its roots back to Windows NT in the early 90s, completely separate from the DOS-based versions that came before. Many underlying features and concepts of Windows NT and 95 are still present in modern-day Windows, and one of them is something people use fairly regularly. Specifically, I'm talking about the drive format utility on Windows 11.

Despite Microsoft overhauling several of its flagship OS' aspects for Windows 11, the drive format tool still uses a dialog box with the same UI and options designed back in 1994. A snippet of code meant to be temporary has persisted to this day, along with a setting created in an era of drastically different storage.

These 5 Windows 11 features have been used since Windows 95

Windows 11 is a modern operating system, but some parts of it have been around for nearly 30 years.

By  João Carrasqueira

Windows' drive format utility has remained virtually unchanged since the 90s

Sometimes, simplicity is all you need

Most of you would be familiar with the drive format utility on Windows. After all, formatting USB drives was fairly common only a few years ago, and it's something that many folks (including yours truly) still rely on when clearing all data on external HDDs and SSDs. Firing up the utility shows a simple UI with a handful of toggles for the format type, disk label, drive capacity, and a couple of other options. You might be surprised to know that this utility looked nearly the same back in 1994, when Microsoft engineer David Plummer created it as a placeholder for Windows NT 4.0. In fact, he also arbitrarily decided on the 32GB partition limit of FAT32, and it stayed that way until Microsoft finally decided to raise this cap up to 2TB earlier this year. But that's a story for another time...

Anyway, the drive formatting utility didn't need to be complicated, so Microsoft probably decided it didn't need to be reworked. In the mid-90s, floppy drives and early hard drives were small enough that the operating system only needed a basic table to track which physical parts of the drive were holding a particular file. To manage this, the file system combined physical disk sectors into "clusters" or "allocation units." And the size of these allocation units is the setting Windows still asks you to choose.

For the uninitiated, an allocation unit is the smallest unit of storage that the OS can assign to a file. The default size is usually 4096 bytes (4KB), which works for most users and storage drives, but you can change it if that suits your use case. A file that's only a few bytes in size will occupy the full 4KB allocation unit. In a nutshell, smaller allocation units are ideal for millions of tiny files, whereas larger sizes work better for a drive with bigger files to minimize wastage.

Windows 95 changed computing forever, and the Virtual OS Museum is the best way to relive it

Things were never the same again

By  João Carrasqueira

The underlying logic changed over the years

Physical sectors went away, but the communication remained the same

As we transitioned from tiny floppy drives to large hard drives with terabytes of storage, the conventional mechanical tracking system had to be replaced. Mapping the exact physical head, cylinder, and sector to parts of a file was no longer efficient on a large drive. So, the industry introduced Logical Block Addressing (LBA) to act as a universal translator. The internal drive controller translates the logical addresses into physical ones whenever Windows accesses data.

Your modern SSD does not store data in "sectors," using pages and blocks instead. However, for compatibility with Windows and legacy software, it emulates logical sectors using LBA, typically using 4KB allocation units. When SSDs arrived on the scene, manufacturers simply designed them to work with LBA instead of forcing operating systems to rewrite how they talked to storage drives.

Hence, the three-decade-old practice of combining drive sectors into allocation units has persisted to this day, despite NAND flash not using sectors at all. This practice maintains compatibility with modern storage, avoids needless rework at the fundamental disk level, and makes no difference to how people use their drives and PCs.

Backwards compatibility often trumps every other consideration

Windows' drive format utility is a prime example of how backwards compatibility is more important than design overhaul. A lot of what goes on underneath the Windows UI you use every day traces back to decades-old code and concepts. Modern operating systems might break down if every new version decided to do things differently just for the sake of it. This is why some things are best left unchanged, even across decades of development.

item.title: Microsoft's new Windows 11 Taskbar Search is the tool I've always wanted
item.itunes:title: Microsoft's new Windows 11 Taskbar Search is the tool I've always wanted
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Copilot in the Windows 11 taskbar's Search runs quick tasks, toggles settings, and finds local files.
  • Hybrid Intelligence lets Copilot access files, run local models, and act on your PC; use the Copilot app for fuller answers.
  • Code can generate Windows apps from a text prompt, and Autopilot automates workflows like finding and attaching a file to an email.

When Copilot arrived on Windows 11, I lamented that it couldn't really help people with simple OS tasks. Back in 2023, it was one of the things I felt Copilot should be able to do in order to succeed on Windows 11.

Well, it seems Microsoft has listened, because it just showed off the power of a brand-new Copilot-enhanced Taskbar search, and as someone who doubted it, I am impressed.

Microsoft showed off the new Copilot-enhanced Taskbar search for Windows 11

It looks pretty powerful

At its Windows and Surface event, Microsoft showed off what this new Copilot-powered Search bar can do. When Copilot first hit Windows 11 PCs, it couldn't handle a lot of simple Windows-based tasks. By comparison, this new Windows Search function seems capable of much more, including adjusting light and dark mode, messaging people, turning on Do Not Disturb, taking screenshots, arranging the desktop, and finding things with a simple text prompt. It's planned to release this fall, so it shouldn't be long until we see it on our PCs, too.

To help the AI find those files you're looking for, Microsoft is introducing a new control layer in Copilot called Hybrid Intelligence. This lets you grant Copilot permission to access files, take actions on Windows, and even use local models to run tasks on your PC. You can toggle these on and off at any time, so you can give the AI running on your machine as much or as little control as you like.

The new taskbar Search plays nicely with Copilot's new sections: Home, Code, and Autopilot. Microsoft calls Home "the new starting point for Copilot," which brings Chat and Cowork into one place. The company showed off what Hybrid Intelligence can do here, such as grabbing local Office files from your PC and opening them up for collaborative work, in case you need more eyes on a document. You can also ask Copilot questions in this new Windows 11 Search, and if you want more detail, you can open the response in the main app for more context.

For Code, Copilot will let people generate Windows-native apps with a single text prompt. It emphasized that "no developer experience is required," that it runs in a secure MXC local sandbox, and that it can even pass work down to other local models when needed. There was also a strong emphasis on people being able to explain what they want from a Windows app and have Code generate it with little to no expertise.

The company's Autopilot demo featured Hybrid Intelligence. The example showed receiving an email from someone asking whether a file was on their system. With Hybrid Intelligence on, the AI searched through the PC, found the file in question, attached it to an email, wrote a draft, and then waited for permission to send it. Autopilot seems to be shaping up to fit its namesake perfectly, letting you ask Copilot to do a specific task on your PC and handle the heavy lifting.

Microsoft's new AI ambitions aren't just restricted to Copilot

It's also working with other agents

If you're not a huge fan of Copilot, Microsoft also took time during its Surface keynote to show how Windows 11 will integrate with third-party agents. The company showed a demo from Perplexity, where someone wrote a prompt asking the agent to take the photos, make smaller, resized copies, and then create a local HTML gallery that supports light and dark mode.

Sure enough, the AI dug through photos, resized them, renamed them, and then presented the user with a completed batch of images. Microsoft emphasized that everything Perplexity did ran locally on the device, which is especially good news for people who'd rather not upload their photos to the cloud.

Windows also added a new "Get Started" flow for getting an agent up and running. If you want to use an AI agent that isn't Copilot, such as Hermes or OpenClaw, Windows 11 gives you a sleek setup flow that lets you pick the model you want, install it, and get started as soon as it's ready.

We finally know the Surface Laptop Ultra’s price and release date, and how its clever breakaway USB-C port works

The Nvidia RTX-powered laptop starts at $2,600 and ships on October 16th.

By  Patrick O'Rourke
